chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Hajjal from Thal'abah ibn Maymun from Imran ibn Ali al-Halabi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'When does the 'Atamah (late evening) prayer become obligatory?' He said, 'When the redness (shafaq) disappears, and the shafaq is the redness.' Ubaidullah said to him, 'May Allah rectify you, for after the disappearance of the redness, a strong light remains that is crosswise (in the sky).' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, the shafaq is only the redness, and the light is not from the shafaq.'

key_terms.الشَّفَقُ: Twilight or the redness in the sky after sunset
key_terms.الْعَتَمَةُ: Late evening prayer (specifically the late Maghrib or Isha prayer in some contexts)
key_terms.مُعْتَرِضٌ: Crosswise or horizontal (referring to the orientation of the light)

ai.seo_question: When does the time for the late evening (Atamah) prayer begin according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the precise definition of *shafaq* (twilight) for the timing of the 'Atamah prayer, distinguishing between the redness of the sky and the residual white light. This distinction is crucial in Shia jurisprudence for determining the exact onset of the late evening prayer time, ensuring it is not delayed until the complete disappearance of all light. The hadith highlights the Imam's attention to astronomical details in establishing religious obligations.
